findings.title: CVE-2026-30612: A vulnerability in Time4Popcorn (PopcornTime)
findings.summary_md: Eye Security published the original advisory for CVE-2026-30612 covering the Windows, macOS, and Android versions of Time4Popcorn, a fork of Popcorn Time. The updater contacts its servers over an insecure channel and accepts an attacker-supplied update; on Windows and macOS the update runs in the background with full privileges (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or root), while on Android the user is prompted to install an APK. The software is abandoned with no update available, and the advisory documents disabling the updater (Windows service 'Update service' via sc.exe, macOS privileged helper PT.updd via launchctl) or removing the software entirely.

findings.title: Operation IXIM: Preventing a botnet of millions of Popcorn Time users
findings.summary_md: Eye Security disclosed Operation IXIM, in which between November 2025 and March 2026 it registered lapsed Time4Popcorn update domains and pushed a harmless update that disabled the updater on more than two million systems. The research traces the flaw to an HTTP updater with no signature verification that executes supplied binaries as SYSTEM or root, and estimates roughly 2.5-3.0 million Windows and 250,000-350,000 macOS hosts. The 15 domains Eye controlled were later transferred to The Shadowserver Foundation for sinkholing.

findings.title: Popcorn Time Updater Hijack: Operation IXIM, CVE-2026-30612, IoCs
findings.summary_md: Safeguard's blog summarizes Operation IXIM and CVE-2026-30612, noting that Eye Security registered 15 lapsed update domains of the abandoned Time4Popcorn fork and pushed a harmless update that switched off the updater on millions of machines. It reconciles the June 2026 advisory with the October 2026 write-up and provides hunt commands and indicators for defenders. The flaw has no patch, so affected users are advised to uninstall the software.

findings.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time app exposed millions of device to RCE attacks
findings.summary_md: Tech Bytes reports that Eye Security neutralized the unencrypted updater flaw in Time4Popcorn, which exposed over three million desktop devices to remote code execution, by intercepting abandoned update infrastructure between November 2025 and March 2026. The updater polled popcorntimeupd.xyz over HTTP and accepted binaries without signature checks, executing them as SYSTEM on Windows or root on macOS. The article advises complete uninstallation and blocking the associated domains.

findings.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time app exposed millions of device to RCE attacks
findings.summary_md: The Verge covers Eye Security's finding that the updater for the Time4Popcorn fork of Popcorn Time remained installed on millions of Windows, macOS, and Android devices, phoning home to abandoned domains over unencrypted HTTP. Researchers registered one domain and pushed an update that disabled the updater, sending over two million update downloads by March before transferring domains to the Shadowserver Foundation. The app also runs an outdated Chrome engine with the sandbox disabled.

findings.title: Popcorn Time updater flaw exposed millions of devices to hijacking
findings.summary_md: CyberInsider reports that Eye Research delivered more than two million update downloads to disable an abandoned Popcorn Time updater that could have allowed attackers to hijack Windows and macOS systems with full privileges. The vulnerability CVE-2026-30612 affected the Time4Popcorn fork, whose update mechanism trusted unsigned executables delivered over unencrypted HTTP, including via expired domains. Android installations received no intervention because updates there require user interaction.
